summary_html: Agency places a child with **relatives or kin caregivers** instead of non-relative foster care. Federal law favors kinship care as least-restrictive, family-preserving placement.

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court held that a third party seeking custody over a fit parent's objection must plead and prove, by a fair preponderance, that continued parental custody would be clearly damaging, injurious or harmful to the child, and that such awards are justified only in exceptional circumstances.
key_cases.relevance: It fixes the constitutional threshold a kin or third-party caregiver must cross before displacing a parent's custody.
key_cases.quote: the petitioner must allege and prove, at the very least, that continued parental custody will be clearly damaging, injurious or harmful to the child

key_cases.holding: The court held § 46b-59 unconstitutional as applied where visitation was ordered over a fit parent's objection without any allegation and proof by clear and convincing evidence of a parent-like relationship and of actual, significant harm to the children if visitation were denied, and it reversed with direction to dismiss the petition.
key_cases.relevance: A relative or kin caregiver cannot obtain court-ordered contact or displace a fit parent's decisions without pleading and proving real and significant harm to the child.
key_cases.quote: The petition must also contain specific, good faith allegations that denial of the visitation will cause real and significant harm to the child.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: A four-Justice plurality held Washington's third-party visitation statute unconstitutional as applied because the trial court gave no special weight to a fit mother's own determination of her daughters' best interests, there being a presumption that fit parents act in their children's best interests.
key_cases.relevance: It is the federal premise underlying Fish v. Fish and Roth v. Weston: a relative or kin caregiver cannot displace a fit parent's judgment on the strength of a best-interests comparison.
key_cases.quote: if a fit parent's decision of the kind at issue here becomes subject to judicial review, the court must accord at least some special weight to the parent's own determination

key_cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that domicile under the Indian Child Welfare Act is a matter of uniform federal law and that twins born off the reservation to reservation-domiciled parents were themselves domiciled on the reservation, so the tribal court had exclusive jurisdiction and the state-court adoption decree had to be vacated.
key_cases.relevance: It shows that ICWA's placement and jurisdictional scheme protects the tribe's own interest in the child and cannot be defeated by the individual parents' choice of caregiver.
key_cases.quote: In enacting the ICWA Congress confirmed that, in child custody proceedings involving Indian children domiciled on the reservation, tribal jurisdiction was exclusive as to the States.

key_cases.holding: The court reversed the Appellate Court, holding that § 46b-129(j)(4) carries a presumption in favor of in-state placement and remanding because the record did not show the trial court applied the correct good cause standard to the out-of-state placement motion.
key_cases.relevance: The presumption favoring in-state placement protects family unity and constrains placement with out-of-state relatives or kin.
key_cases.quote: Upon review of the record, we cannot be confident that the trial court applied the correct legal standard to adjudicate the petitioner's motion for out-of-state placement.

timeline_requirements.starts_from: Issuance of the ex parte order of temporary custody or order to appear

notice_requirements.timing: At the commencement of any proceeding on behalf of a neglected, uncared-for or abused child or youth, and again at the preliminary hearing on an order of temporary custody or order to appear
content_required: The parent or guardian has the right to counsel and must be so informed by the judge
If the parent or guardian is unable to afford counsel, counsel will be provided
The parent or guardian has the rights of confrontation and cross-examination

The court may also appoint counsel for the parent or guardian without a request if it determines the interests of justice so require (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 46b-136(a)); in a proceeding in which the custody of a child is at issue the judge must provide an attorney for the child

Cost of appointed counsel in the civil juvenile session is shared as agreed by the Division of Public Defender Services and the Judicial Department, and the court may order a party found able to pay to reimburse that cost (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 46b-136(b)(1))
notice_requirements.defective_notice_consequence: Not specified in Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 46b-135 or 46b-136

statutory_basis.citation_text: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 46b-135(b) (right to counsel and cross-examination); see also § 46b-136 (appointment of attorney; payment) and § 46b-129(c)(1) (advisement at the preliminary hearing)

notice_requirements.timing: In any involuntary Superior Court proceeding for foster care placement of, or termination of parental rights to, an Indian child, once the court knows or has reason to know an Indian child is involved
content_required: Notice of the right of intervention

If the parent, Indian custodian or tribe cannot be identified or located, like notice to the Bureau of Indian Affairs Regional Director or Secretary (federally recognized tribe) or to the Commissioner of Children and Families (tribe recognized by the state of Connecticut), who then has 15 days to give the required notice
notice_requirements.defective_notice_consequence: The Indian child, parent, Indian custodian or tribe may petition to invalidate a foster care placement or termination of parental rights action that violated state or federal law (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 46b-116n)

statutory_basis.citation_text: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 46b-116d (required notice to Indian parent, Indian custodian and Indian tribe of state foster care and termination of parental rights proceedings), Connecticut Indian Child Welfare Act
